name: Glucomannan

lead: Glucomannan is a soluble fibre from the konjac plant, used in shirataki noodles and sold as a supplement. Dieters take it to feel full on fewer calories while getting leaner.

It absorbs water and forms a viscous gel in the stomach, which proponents say increases fullness and slows nutrient absorption. A meta-analysis found a non-significant weight difference of about 0.22 kg versus placebo, while the EU has allowed a weight-loss claim since 2010 for people on calorie-restricted diets. A meta-analysis also suggests it may lower LDL cholesterol by up to 10 percent.

paras: It is taken as capsules, powder or in konjac foods before meals, always with plenty of fluid, as part of a calorie-controlled diet. Health Canada advises against taking it at bedtime.

Taken with too little water, glucomannan products can cause choking or bowel obstruction. Common effects are diarrhoea, belching and bloating. The US FDA barred konjac jelly candies from import in 2001 over choking hazards.

angle.text: Dieters take glucomannan, a konjac fibre that forms a gel in the stomach, to feel fuller and eat less while getting leaner. Meta-analyses of weight loss report small changes.

lead: Glucomannan is a water-soluble polysaccharide and dietary fibre made of beta-1,4-linked mannose and glucose units, found in the cell walls of several plants. The konjac corm is its main commercial source, at about 40 percent by dry weight.[1][2] When mixed with water it absorbs many times its own weight and forms a thick gel.

People use it to lean out by eating less: as a capsule or powder taken with water before meals to feel fuller, or as the main ingredient of shirataki noodles and rice substitutes that supply volume with almost no digestible calories.[1][3] Chewing less food-energy while feeling satisfied is the chain by which it is meant to support fat loss, a lower body-fat percentage and a leaner face and physique. It is also sold for constipation and cholesterol, and konjac sponges made from the same corm are used for gentle facial cleansing.[1][2]

Research on its weight effect has produced a range of results. A 2014 meta-analysis of eight randomised trials found a mean difference of 0.22 kg against placebo that was not statistically significant, while a 2021 meta-analysis of 67 trials reported a 1.27 kg reduction, and a 2023 network meta-analysis reported 1.36 kg.[4][5] Trials and meta-analyses also report lower total and LDL cholesterol.[4] Regulators differ: the EU has allowed a weight-loss claim since 2010 under defined conditions, while the US FTC has pursued some supplement marketers over their claims.[1]

paras: Capsules and powders are marketed for weight loss and appetite control.[1] The stated mechanism is that the fibre forms a gel when mixed with water, takes up space in the stomach, stays there longer than water alone and so produces a sense of fullness after eating less; it may also slow the absorption of nutrients.[1] People cutting body fat use it for this reason, usually alongside a calorie-controlled diet, and reviews of weight-loss supplements treat it as a satiety-type fibre in the same family as psyllium and guar gum.[5]

A separate use is volume eating. Shirataki noodles are about 97 percent water and 3 percent konjac, so they contribute little digestible carbohydrate or energy, and dieters sometimes substitute them for wheat or rice noodles.[3] On T Nation, posters have asked about konjac or glucomannan pasta as a near-zero-calorie option and recommended glucomannan noodles in a diet plan.[6][7]

Products are also sold for constipation and to lower cholesterol; in Europe and Canada they can be marketed with those claims.[1] A 2025 double-blind trial in elite male taekwondo athletes with functional constipation found that eight weeks of konjac glucomannan improved symptom and quality-of-life scores and bowel-movement frequency compared with placebo.[8] A review of non-drug approaches to childhood constipation lists glucomannan among fibre supplements with emerging evidence in children.[9]

Several meta-analyses report lipid effects. A GRADE-assessed 2024 meta-analysis of randomised trials found lower total cholesterol and LDL cholesterol with glucomannan and no significant change in triglycerides, and a 2023 meta-analysis of six trials in type 2 diabetes reported lower cholesterol, fasting glucose and insulin.[4] Wikipedia notes that one study found higher triglycerides in people taking it.[1]

Dried konjac corm is used to make konjac sponges for gentle facial cleansing, and the same flour is used as a vegan gelatin substitute and as a wet-strength additive in Japanese hand papermaking.[2] Glucomannan is also an additive (E425(ii)) used as a thickener and emulsifier and is fed to farm animals to improve feed conversion.[1]

The konjac plant was domesticated in southwest China roughly 2,000 years ago, and early growers made the raw corm edible by repeatedly boiling it with alkaline ash water. The earliest clear record of food use dates to the Western Jin dynasty (265 to 317 AD), and Japan has eaten it since at least the sixth century, first as a medicinal food.[2] In 1776 Nakajima Toemon developed a method of making konjac flour, which made the product easier to store and transport.[2]

Konjac became a regional staple in Japan, where konnyaku and shirataki are used in dishes such as oden and sukiyaki, and in Sichuan and neighbouring provinces, where it stands in for beef tripe in hot pot.[2] Konjac fruit jelly has been sold since 1979 and later became the subject of choking-related warnings.[2] As a supplement, glucomannan reached Western weight-loss markets in capsule and powder form under brand names such as Lipozene, while shirataki noodles spread through low-carbohydrate and low-calorie diet culture.[1][3]

Glucomannan's backbone is composed of D-mannose and D-glucose in a ratio of roughly 1.6 to 1, with about 8 percent branching through beta-1,6-glucosyl linkages.[1] It occurs in konjac, in salep (ground orchid root), in conifer wood and in the cell walls of microbes. Plant cell-wall reviews describe glucomannan as a hemicellulose component of secondary walls, and a structural review covers the mannan-degrading enzymes that act on it.[1][10][11]

Konjac glucomannan is used as a thickener, a gelatin substitute and the base of shirataki noodles. Salep gives Turkish dondurma ice cream its chewy texture, although the orchid species involved are protected in the EU.[1]

Weight-loss findings differ between analyses. A 2014 systematic review in the Journal of the American College of Nutrition identified 18 trials, included nine, and in a random-effects meta-analysis of eight randomised trials found a mean difference of 0.22 kg versus placebo (95% CI -0.62 to 0.19); the authors reported no statistically significant weight loss and called for more rigorous trials. A 2020 critical review of supplements marketed for weight loss in people with obesity found insufficient evidence for most of them, with a possible exception for glucomannan in the form of PGX. A 2016 review of newer weight-management supplements, including glucomannan, concluded that evidence was insufficient to recommend their use.

Later pooled analyses report small reductions. A 2021 meta-analysis of 67 placebo-controlled trials of isolated-compound supplements found glucomannan reduced weight by 1.27 kg (95% CI -2.45 to -0.09) versus placebo, below the authors' 2.5 kg threshold for clinical significance.[4] A 2023 network meta-analysis of 111 trials ranked glucomannan at -1.36 kg (95% CI -2.17 to -0.54) with low certainty of evidence, compared with -3.70 kg for psyllium at moderate certainty.[5] A 2022 meta-analysis of 27 trials of isolated soluble fibre supplements in adults with overweight or obesity found an average 1.25 kg reduction, covering soluble fibre in general rather than glucomannan alone.[4]

A 2024 randomised double-blind trial of a combined glucomannan, inulin and psyllium product in 112 adults with obesity and certain gene variants reported body-weight differences of 4.9 percent versus placebo over 180 days. It was funded by the product's makers, and 74.6 percent of the supplement group reported gastrointestinal events.[12]

Glucomannan has also been tested for blood-sugar effects. Small randomised trials report that it reduced rises in plasma glucose and insulin and affected triglycerides after a rice gruel test meal, and a randomised trial in type 2 diabetes reported effects on the hormone ghrelin.[1][13][14]

Common effects are diarrhoea, belching and bloating; reviews of randomised trials report abdominal discomfort, diarrhoea and constipation.[1] Because the fibre swells, products can cause choking or blockage of the throat, oesophagus or intestine if taken without enough fluid. A Health Canada advisory cited on Wikipedia states that tablets, capsules and powders carry potential for harm unless taken with at least 250 ml of water or other fluid, and advises against taking them just before bed.[1]

Konjac fruit jelly snacks have been linked to choking deaths. The US FDA issued warnings in 2001 and barred a number of such products from import, while the EU and Australia banned them; in Japan, 17 people died from choking on konjac between 1995 and 2008, and a major manufacturer paused jelly sales in 2008.[1][2] A 1999 choking incident in California led to a judgment of 16.7 million dollars against a Taiwanese manufacturer.[2]

The US FTC or FDA has found several supplement companies, including Vitacost, PediaLean and BioTrim, to have at some point violated federal law, and Obesity Research Institute, which marketed FiberThin, Zylotrim, Propolene and Lipozene, settled FTC charges and paid 1.5 million dollars in consumer redress over weight-loss claims.[1] The EU has permitted a weight-loss claim for glucomannan since 2010, following a European Food Safety Authority opinion, and EFSA re-evaluated konjac gum and konjac glucomannan as food additives in 2017.[1][15]

Glucomannan appears in leanmaxxing discussions as a cheap OTC appetite aid, often alongside prescription weight-loss drugs. A looksmax.org member posting a leanmaxxing field report that mixed an Ozempic order, another prescription drug and glucomannan described it as technically available everywhere but, in his words, working 'more as a placebo' while still ordering extra.[16] On T Nation it has been mentioned for appetite suppression late in a diet, for bowel regularity, and as a cholesterol-lowering add-on by a user on testosterone therapy.[17][18][19]
Konjac noodles are discussed as food rather than as a supplement, as a way to keep meal volume high on very low calories.[6][7]

Human trials and reviews include the 2014 meta-analysis of eight randomised trials (no significant weight difference versus placebo), the 2021 meta-analysis of 67 trials (1.27 kg reduction),[4] the 2023 network meta-analysis of 111 trials,[5] a 2024 randomised trial of a fibre blend in 112 adults,[12] a 2025 randomised trial in athletes with constipation,[8] and lipid and type 2 diabetes meta-analyses.[4]

Registered trials include studies of glucomannan on body weight in overweight adults (NCT01485718, NCT01709955) and in overweight or obese children (NCT02280772, 96 participants), childhood functional constipation (NCT01151878, 92 participants), abdominal pain-related functional disorders in children (NCT01495806, 89 participants), satiety from viscous fibre foods (NCT02134938) and glucose homeostasis after gastric bypass (NCT02336438).[20][21][22][23][24][25][26] Results from several of these have not been published.

lore.intro: On looksmax.org and T Nation, glucomannan is discussed as a cheap appetite aid for cutting, as konjac noodles and as a digestive fibre, with users divided on how much it does.[16][6][17]
